We studied a population of the benthic cichlid Trematocara variabile from the deep waters of Lake Tanganyika, where individuals are rarely encountered above depths of fifty meters. Field surveys revealed that neonates emerge from demersal eggs weighing just 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], a remarkably small initial wet weight at birth that reflects the tiny size of the yolky, adhesive eggs typical of lacustrine cichlids. Yolk-sac larvae absorb their endogenous reserves over a period of several days before initiating exogenous feeding. The measured total length at puberty for this species is 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation under the stable thermal conditions of the lake's hypolimnion, which remain near 25 °C [T = 25 °C] throughout the year. This constant temperature regime appears to influence several key life-history parameters by ensuring a predictable metabolic environment.

As juveniles grow, their body mass increases steadily until they reach the asymptote characteristic of fully grown adults in this population. The ultimate wet weight recorded for large, reproductively viable individuals is 34.6 grams [Wwi = 34.6 grams], a value that aligns with the slender, elongated body shape of this species compared to more deep-bodied Tanganyikan cichlids. This maximum adult body mass is attained at the ultimate total length of 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], which represents the largest size class routinely observed during benthic trawl surveys. Interestingly, the wet weight at puberty, when gonadal recrudescence is first detectable through histological examination, is approximately 3.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.1 grams]. This represents a considerable investment in somatic growth before the onset of reproductive activity, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy in a relatively stable deep-water environment.

During the spawning season, gravid females migrate to shallower rocky habitats to deposit their clutch. The maximum reproductive rate observed in this species, extrapolated from related lacustrine cichlids under controlled conditions at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is reflected in a combination of moderate clutch sizes and multiple spawning events spread across the breeding season. Clutch size typically ranges from 10 to 25 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 10 to 25 eggs per spawning event], and females may release between three and five clutches per year [F_R_i = between three and five clutches per year], depending on nutritional condition and access to suitable nesting crevices. The protracted breeding period is an adaptation to the relatively low productivity of the deep benthic zone, where energy resources are diffuse.

Longevity estimates for Trematocara variabile indicate that these fish lead relatively long lives compared to many other cichlids of similar body size. Under the stable thermal conditions of their deep-water habitat, which remains consistently around 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded approaches six years [am = six years]. This extended lifespan is likely linked to the low metabolic demands of the deep benthos and the absence of significant predation pressure from pelagic piscivores at these depths. Senescent individuals are occasionally recovered during sampling, showing signs of physiological deterioration consistent with age-related death. The combination of a small adult body mass of approximately 34.6 grams and a lifespan of six years places Trematocara variabile on the relatively slow end of the cichlid life-history continuum, where delayed reproduction and moderate fecundity are common.

The overall life-history syndrome of Trematocara variabile, characterized by a modest pubertal length of 8 centimeters, a maximum length of 17 centimeters, and an adult mass just over 34 grams, reflects the constraints of a stable but energetically limited environment. Interestingly, the wet weight at first reproductive maturity of 3.1 grams [Wwp = 3.1 grams] is reached only after several months of juvenile growth, a delay that allows the fish to build sufficient body reserves. This suite of traits—small birth mass of 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], gradual attainment of puberty at 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters] total length, and a maximum lifespan of six years—positions Trematocara variabile as a typical deep-water specialist adapted to the cold, constant temperatures of the Lake Tanganyika profundal zone.
